summary: This informational memo from the Independent Stream asks whether the Domain Name System should be redesigned and replaced, or whether the community should draw clear lines about what DNS should and should not do. It argues that expectations around privacy, authorization, special names, character encoding, matching and the root have changed a lot since the original design. It poses the question rather than defining a protocol.

eli5.summary: The phone book for the internet is very old. This paper asks whether we should keep patching it or build a new one, and what jobs it should really do.

questions: what are the problems with dns today
what is wrong with internationalized domain names in dns
subtitle: Can the 30-year-old domain name system be redesigned, or should its scope be limited?

tldr.problem: The Domain Name System was designed nearly 30 years ago with assumptions that no longer match how the Internet is used. New requirements around privacy, internationalization, performance, and security are straining its original design.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC catalogs 15 major tensions in DNS (from multi-type queries to root server management) and asks whether the Internet community should redesign DNS from scratch or draw clear boundaries about what DNS should and should not do.
tldr.outcome: The document does not propose solutions, but rather frames the debate: either accept that a 30-year-old architecture has limitations, or invest in a new system designed for today's needs.

today: RFC 8324 is an Informational RFC published on the Independent Submission stream. It has not been obsoleted and stands as an open question rather than a proposal, inviting the Internet community to debate whether DNS redesign is overdue.

sections.title: The Central Question
sections.content:
RFC 8324 is not a technical specification; it is a thoughtful argument asking whether the time has come to redesign the Domain Name System (DNS) entirely. The DNS has been the Internet's directory service since the early 1980s, and it has been extraordinarily successful. However, the document argues that expectations of what DNS should do have changed so much in the last 15 years that the system is now experiencing stresses it was never designed to handle.

The author poses three possible paths forward: redesign DNS from scratch to match contemporary needs, set clear boundaries on what DNS is not meant to do and handle those tasks elsewhere, or accept the limitations and design better workarounds.
sections.eli5: After 30 years, the internet's phone book is struggling. This paper asks if we should fix it by replacing it, by saying 'that is not what a phone book is for,' or by just learning to live with what we have.

sections.title: A System Built for a Different Era
sections.content:
DNS was designed in the early 1980s to replace flat host tables with a hierarchical, distributed system. It solved the problem of how to manage hostnames at internet scale. Since then, it has been extended with new record types (MX for mail, CNAME for aliases, DNSSEC for security, and many others), but the fundamental design remains rooted in 1980s assumptions.

The document points out that early changes, like the shift from the MD/MF mail system to MX records, or the later addition of IPv6 support, were incremental. What has changed is the scope of what people want DNS to do: not just name-to-address lookup, but privacy protection, content localization, policy enforcement, and much more.
sections.eli5: DNS was built when the internet was small and simple. Now people want it to do jobs it was never designed for, like keeping lookups private or managing thousands of names.

sections.title: The Major Stresses: A Few Examples
sections.content:
The document identifies 15 specific areas of tension. A few are particularly revealing:

Privacy and query visibility: DNS queries are sent in cleartext and can be intercepted. Proposals like DNS-over-TLS add encryption, but the author argues this is a patch, not a designed-in feature.

Internationalization: The original DNS supported only ASCII letters, digits, and hyphens. Adding support for non-ASCII names required complex workarounds (IDNA). Matching rules are still inconsistent, and variant names (like simplified vs. traditional Chinese characters) are difficult to handle.

Performance and transport: DNS was designed for short queries that fit in a single UDP packet. Modern requests, especially with DNSSEC signatures, often exceed 512 bytes and require TCP or fragmented UDP, reducing reliability.

Scope creep: Applications use DNS for tasks beyond naming: mail routing (MX), service location (SRV), authentication (SPF, DKIM), and arbitrary data (TXT records). Each addition stretches the design.
sections.eli5: DNS is used for things it was not meant for. Some examples: keeping queries secret, writing names in Chinese, sending big answers, and storing mail rules.

sections.title: The Deeper Design Tensions
sections.content:
Beyond specific features, the document identifies philosophical tensions that no patch can fully resolve:

Identifiers vs. brands: DNS was designed for unambiguous technical identifiers (like server names). Today, companies want their brands and products in DNS (like a company named "3M" or symbols in domain names). These goals—unambiguous identity vs. human-friendly expression—are fundamentally in conflict within the same system.

Centralized control: DNS requires a centrally managed root. Modern cryptography (blockchain approaches have been suggested) might allow decentralized root management, but DNS's current architecture depends on central authority.

Special names and private namespaces: Organizations want to use DNS for internal-only names, special top-level domains for testing, or reserved names that bypass normal lookup. Each workaround adds complexity.
sections.eli5: Some problems go deeper than features. For example, DNS wants to be both a technical tool and a way to write brand names. These goals pull in different directions.

sections.title: Moving Forward: Redesign or Redefine?
sections.content:
The RFC does not propose a new DNS, but it does sketch the options. One approach is to accept that DNS is a system for network resource naming and use a separate search and disambiguation layer (like a search engine) for human-friendly name resolution. Another is to design a new system with privacy, internationalization, and flexible policy as core features rather than bolted-on extensions. A third is to simply acknowledge that DNS has limits and design other systems to handle privacy, service discovery, and content distribution.

The document notes that 30 years ago, many proposed DNS features were abandoned when they proved unworkable (like the MD and MF record types). The same will likely happen with newer proposals. The question is whether the cost of repeated patches and incremental band-aids is higher than the cost of a redesign.
sections.eli5: Either redesign DNS from scratch, split its jobs among different systems, or accept its limits and build better workarounds elsewhere.
